title: ITC Grand Chola Launches Cholatails — a Cocktail Menu Rooted in the Chola Dynasty and Tamil Soil
excerpt: The Chennai hotel's new beverage programme uses nannari, tamarind, long pepper, and even Bovonto to build drinks that could only exist in Tamil Nadu — a departure from luxury hotels' usual international playbook.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • ITC Grand Chola launched Cholatails, a cocktail menu inspired by the Chola dynasty.
  • The menu features local Tamil ingredients like nannari, tamarind, and Bovonto.
  • Signature drinks include Chukku Kaapi and the nostalgic 1958 mocktail.
  • Cholatails aims to create a unique local cocktail identity for luxury hotels.
  • The menu reflects a shift towards regional authenticity in Indian dining.

Key Takeaways

  • ITC Grand Chola in Chennai has launched Cholatails, a cocktail and mocktail menu inspired by the Chola dynasty
  • The menu was developed in collaboration with Mumbai-based beverage consultancy The Happy High
  • Drinks use hyper-local Tamil ingredients including nannari, tamarind, long pepper, coconut water, and Bovonto
  • Standout creations include Chukku Kaapi (cognac meets filter coffee) and 1958 (a Bovonto-based mocktail)
  • The menu is served at The Cheroot Malt & Cigar Lounge inside the ITC Grand Chola

Walk into The Cheroot Malt & Cigar Lounge at ITC Grand Chola in Chennai and the drink menu will stop you. It is not the usual litany of international cocktails with an Indian twist. It is something more specific, more rooted, and considerably more ambitious — a beverage programme that draws its vocabulary from the Chola dynasty, its ingredients from Tamil soil, and its technique from contemporary mixology.

The menu is called Cholatails, and it represents one of the most deliberate attempts by a luxury Indian hotel to build a cocktail identity that is irreducibly local.

A Kingdom in a Glass

The Cholatails programme was developed in collaboration with The Happy High, a Mumbai-based beverage consultancy led by Ajit Balgi that has built a reputation for creating concept-driven drink menus across India's top hotels and restaurants. For ITC Grand Chola, the brief was clear: create a menu that could only exist in Chennai.

> **""We wanted every drink to tell a story that begins and ends in Tamil Nadu," says Ajit Balgi of The Happy High."**

The result is a collection of cocktails and mocktails that reach deep into Tamil Nadu's pantry. Nannari — the fragrant sarsaparilla root used in traditional South Indian summer coolers — appears in multiple preparations. Tamarind, long pepper (pippali), coconut water, guava, and jaggery form the flavour backbone. Even Bovonto, the cult-favourite grape-flavoured soft drink born in Thoothukudi in 1958, gets its moment.

"We wanted every drink to tell a story that begins and ends in Tamil Nadu," says Ajit Balgi of The Happy High. "The Chola dynasty gave us the narrative frame. The land gave us the ingredients."

The Drinks That Stand Out

Chukku Kaapi is the menu's signature statement — a drink that bridges two of Tamil Nadu's most powerful flavour traditions. Cognac meets South Indian filter coffee, tempered with chukku (dry ginger), and served in a way that evokes the brass tumblers of a traditional coffee house. It is both deeply familiar and entirely new.

Pippali, named for the long pepper that was once a prized trade commodity of the Chola empire, builds its heat slowly — a warm, tingling spice that unfolds over the length of the drink rather than hitting all at once. Puli takes tamarind from its usual role as a cooking staple and reframes it as a cocktail ingredient, balanced with citrus and a restrained sweetness.

The Thalaivar Martini — a nod to Tamil cinema's culture of larger-than-life heroes — is the menu's most theatrical offering, built for the drinker who wants flavour and presence in equal measure.

Among the mocktails, 1958 stands apart. Named for the year Bovonto was created, it takes the nostalgic grape soda and elevates it into a grown-up preparation that retains the drink's essential character while adding layers of complexity. For anyone who grew up drinking Bovonto from a glass bottle at a railway station, it is an immediate emotional trigger.

Why This Matters for Indian Dining

India's luxury hotel bars have historically defaulted to international cocktail grammar — a negroni here, a whisky sour there, perhaps with a curry leaf garnish or a chai syrup to signal locality. Cholatails does something different. It starts with the local and builds outward, treating Tamil ingredients and cultural references as the foundation rather than the garnish.

This approach reflects a broader shift in Indian hospitality. As diners become more knowledgeable and more willing to pay for distinctiveness, hotels are recognising that genuine regional identity is a competitive advantage, not a limitation. A drink made with nannari root and pippali cannot be replicated in a bar in London or New York. That specificity is the point.

Shaariq Akhtar, General Manager of ITC Grand Chola, frames it in terms of the hotel's identity. The ITC Grand Chola was conceived as an architectural tribute to the Chola dynasty — its pillared corridors, bronze sculptures, and Dravidian design motifs are central to the guest experience. A cocktail menu that extends that narrative into the glass is, in this context, a natural completion rather than a marketing exercise.

The Bigger Picture for NRI Visitors

For diaspora visitors returning to Chennai, the menu offers something that international Indian restaurants rarely can: drinks that taste of a specific place and a specific memory. The flavours of nannari sherbet and filter coffee and tamarind rasam are not generic Indian references — they are Tamil markers that connect to childhood, to grandparents' kitchens, to summers spent in the South.

The Cholatails menu is available at The Cheroot Malt & Cigar Lounge at ITC Grand Chola, Chennai. Pricing varies by preparation, with cocktails in the ₹800 to ₹1,200 range and mocktails at ₹400 to ₹600.
